facts.statehood_note: One of the original 13; Pennsylvania ratified the U.S. Constitution on December 12, 1787, the 2nd state to do so, five days after Delaware. Its official name is the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.
facts.nickname: The Keystone State (also called the Quaker State)
borders: Lake Erie (with Ontario, Canada, across the lake)
facts.name_origin: William Penn suggested "Sylvania," from the Latin word silva ("forest"). King Charles II named it Pennsylvania, "Penn's Woods," to honor Penn's father, Admiral William Penn.

government.legislature: Pennsylvania General Assembly (it began as the colony's Provincial Assembly in 1682, has been called the General Assembly since 1776, and has had two chambers since 1791)
government.chambers: Pennsylvania State Senate (50 senators, 4-year terms) and Pennsylvania House of Representatives (203 members, 2-year terms), meeting in the State Capitol in Harrisburg
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; may serve two terms in a row). The lieutenant governor runs on the same ticket as the governor.
government.courts: Supreme Court of Pennsylvania (7 justices, 10-year terms; voters then decide in a yes-or-no retention vote whether each justice stays, and justices must retire at 75). Dating to 1684, it is called the oldest appellate court in the nation, and it hears appeals from the Superior Court and the Commonwealth Court.
government.local: 67 counties, divided into municipalities that are cities, boroughs, or townships.
government.constitution: Pennsylvania has had constitutions in 1776, 1790, 1838, 1874, and 1968; the current one dates from 1968. Before 1776 the colony was governed under William Penn's Frames of Government and his 1701 Charter of Privileges.
government.kid_line: "All men are born equally free and independent, and have certain inherent and indefeasible rights, among which are those of enjoying and defending life and liberty, of acquiring, possessing and protecting property and reputation, and of pursuing their own happiness." (Pennsylvania Constitution, Article I, Section 1).

long_ago.about: The Lenape spoke an Algonquian language and lived in Lenapehoking, which covered eastern Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, and parts of New York. Women grew the Three Sisters (corn, beans, and squash) and owned their own property, children belonged to their mother's clan, and village leaders called sachems listened to councils of elders.

The Susquehannock spoke an Iroquoian language and lived in villages along the lower Susquehanna River, protected by double walls of logs. Families shared longhouses; women farmed corn, beans, and squash while men hunted, traded, and fished with weirs, and villages moved about every 25 years when the soil wore out.

When Europeans arrived, Haudenosaunee lands reached south into what is now northwestern Pennsylvania, and around 1700 their power stretched along both sides of the Allegheny Mountains into the Ohio Valley.
Descendants of Susquehannock and Seneca people lived at Conestoga Town in Lancaster County until 1763.

first_peoples.today_note: Pennsylvania has no federally recognized tribe based in the state today. The Lenape were pushed west in the 1700s and 1800s, and their three federally recognized nations are the Delaware Nation (Anadarko, Oklahoma), the Delaware Tribe of Indians (Bartlesville, Oklahoma), and the Stockbridge-Munsee Community (Wisconsin). In 2000 the Delaware Nation received 11.5 acres in Thornbury Township, Delaware County, Pennsylvania.
sites: Penn Treaty Park (Philadelphia), where a peace treaty with the Lenape was made in 1682
Gettysburg National Military Park and Gettysburg National Cemetery
Independence Hall (Philadelphia), where the Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution were signed
Stevens and Smith Historic Site (Lancaster), with a hidden cistern used on the Underground Railroad

history.event: The Lenape live in the east, in Lenapehoking, and the Susquehannock farm along the lower Susquehanna River.
English explorer John Smith meets about 60 Susquehannock men at the mouth of the Susquehanna River.
Weakened by disease and years of war with the Haudenosaunee, the Susquehannock leave their river village and move south into Maryland.

King Charles II signs a charter giving William Penn the land on March 4, 1681. In 1682 Penn founds Philadelphia, buys land from the Lenape, and makes a peace treaty with them, and the first legislature meets in December.
The ship Isabella arrives in Philadelphia carrying about 150 enslaved Africans; Penn himself owned and traded enslaved people.
Francis Daniel Pastorius and three other men of Germantown write the first American public document to protest slavery. Colony leaders reject it.
In the Walking Purchase, colony leaders use an old deed the Lenape reject to take a huge area of Lenape land, a deal now widely seen as fraud.
The Paxton Boys kill about 20 Conestoga people at Conestoga Town and the Lancaster workhouse. Benjamin Franklin condemns the killings, and in 1764 he helps stop the group's march on Philadelphia.
The Pennsylvania Abolition Society, the first American abolition society, is founded in Philadelphia.
The Second Continental Congress adopts the Declaration of Independence in Philadelphia, and Pennsylvania writes its first state constitution.
The Continental Congress flees Philadelphia, and Lancaster serves as the U.S. capital for one day, September 27.

On March 1, Pennsylvania passes An Act for the Gradual Abolition of Slavery, the first such law in America. Children born to enslaved mothers after the act would be free at age 28, and no new enslaved people could be brought in. Slavery ended slowly: 64 people were still enslaved in 1840, and none by 1850.
The U.S. Constitution is written and signed at the Pennsylvania State House (Independence Hall); on December 12 Pennsylvania becomes the 2nd state to ratify it.

About 350,000 Pennsylvanians serve in the Union army, including 8,600 African American volunteers. Before and during the war, places like Lancaster's Bethel AME Church help freedom seekers on the Underground Railroad.
The Battle of Gettysburg (July 1 to 3) leaves more than 50,000 soldiers killed, wounded, or missing; on November 19 Abraham Lincoln gives the 271-word Gettysburg Address.
Lancaster's Thaddeus Stevens, a leader in Congress, helps shape the Fourteenth Amendment and pushes for equal rights during Reconstruction.

trailblazers.name: William Penn
trailblazers.text: Penn founded Pennsylvania and Philadelphia, and his Frame of Government promised freedom of religion and trial by jury. He made a peace treaty with the Lenape in 1682, but he also owned and traded enslaved people.

trailblazers.name: Francis Daniel Pastorius and the Germantown petitioners
trailblazers.text: In 1688 Pastorius, Garret Hendericks, and Derick and Abraham op den Graeff of Germantown wrote the first American public document protesting slavery. Colony leaders turned it down, but it is remembered as a brave first step.

trailblazers.name: Benjamin Franklin
trailblazers.group: Philadelphia printer, scientist, and Founding Father
trailblazers.text: Franklin invented the lightning rod, bifocals, and the Franklin stove, started a library and a fire company, and signed both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution. He owned at least seven enslaved people, later turned against slavery, freed the people he held, and led the Pennsylvania Abolition Society from 1787 to 1790.

trailblazers.name: Thaddeus Stevens
trailblazers.text: In 1835 Stevens defended Pennsylvania's new free public schools, and in Congress he fought slavery and helped shape the Fourteenth Amendment. He chose to be buried in a cemetery open to people of every race; his gravestone says "Equality of man before his Creator."

trailblazers.name: K. Leroy Irvis
trailblazers.text: Irvis led a 1947 protest against hiring discrimination by Pittsburgh department stores and served in the Pennsylvania House from 1958 to 1988. In 1977 he became Speaker, the first African American speaker of any state legislature since Reconstruction, and he helped create the state's community colleges and its Human Relations Commission.

trailblazers.name: William Still
trailblazers.group: Black American man, Underground Railroad leader
trailblazers.text: Still chaired the Vigilance Committee of the Pennsylvania Anti-Slavery Society in Philadelphia and helped nearly 1,000 freedom seekers, including Harriet Tubman, whom he met and assisted in the early 1850s. He secretly recorded their names and stories, sometimes hiding his journal in a cemetery, and in 1872 he published The Underground Railroad, a 780-page book of their accounts.

trailblazers.name: Frances Ellen Watkins Harper
trailblazers.group: Black American woman, poet and abolitionist
trailblazers.text: Born free in Baltimore, Maryland, Frances Ellen Watkins Harper settled in Philadelphia after an 1853 Maryland law barred free Black people from entering that state. She lived in an Underground Railroad station, helped freedom seekers alongside William Still, and was hired as a lecturer by the Pennsylvania Anti-Slavery Society. A famous poet and author, she died in Philadelphia in 1911.

landforms: Appalachian Mountains (through the middle of the state)
waters: about 86,000 miles of rivers and streams
geography.regions: Pennsylvania's natural regions are the Erie Plain along Lake Erie, the Allegheny Plateau, the Ridge and Valley, the Piedmont, and the Atlantic Coastal Plain, with the Appalachian Mountains running through the center of the state.

ecosystems.name: Forests
ecosystems.about: About 59% of Pennsylvania is covered by forest, a fit for "Penn's Woods"; the Allegheny is the state's only national forest.

ecosystems.name: The Susquehanna River
ecosystems.about: At 444 miles it is the longest river on the East Coast; it drains nearly half of Pennsylvania, gives the Chesapeake Bay about half its fresh water, and is famous for smallmouth bass.

science.weather: Most of Pennsylvania has cold winters and hot, humid summers. Areas near Lake Erie can get more than 100 inches of snow a year, and tornadoes happen every year (30 were recorded in 2011).
science.resources: Coal mining began in the mid-1700s, the U.S. oil industry was born in western Pennsylvania in boom towns like Titusville, and Pittsburgh became a steel center; Hershey is home to one of the world's largest chocolate makers.
science.highlight: Benjamin Franklin's electricity science: in Philadelphia, Franklin studied electricity and invented the lightning rod, which protects buildings from lightning strikes (he may have done his famous kite experiment in June 1752).

g3_ss.title: Pennsylvania's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Map Harrisburg, Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, and the student's town; learn the General Assembly (Senate 50, House 203), the governor, and the Supreme Court; talk about what a commonwealth is.

g3_ss.title: Pennsylvania's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Meet the Lenape and Susquehannock; compare Three Sisters farming, longhouses, and clans; find where Lenape nations live today in Oklahoma, Wisconsin, and Ontario.

g3_ss.title: Pennsylvania Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Timeline cards for the Germantown petitioners, Benjamin Franklin, Thaddeus Stevens, and K. Leroy Irvis; students write one sentence on how each worked for fairness.

g45_ss.title: Pennsylvania's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Lenapehoking and Lenape government, Susquehannock towns and John Smith's 1608 meeting, the Haudenosaunee, and how disease and war changed the region.

g45_ss.title: Penn's Woods: Colony to Commonwealth
g45_ss.plan: The 1681 charter, the 1682 treaty, slavery in the colony and the 1688 Germantown protest, the Walking Purchase, the 1763 Conestoga killings, and the 1775 Abolition Society.

g45_ss.title: Pennsylvania 1776–1877
g45_ss.plan: The Declaration and Constitution in Philadelphia, ratification as the 2nd state, the Underground Railroad in Lancaster, the Civil War and Gettysburg, and Thaddeus Stevens in Reconstruction.

g3_sci.title: Penn's Woods
g3_sci.plan: Why 59% of the state is forest; trees, leaves, and the animals that need them; a backyard tree study.

g3_sci.title: River Journey
g3_sci.plan: Follow the Susquehanna from New York through Pennsylvania to the Chesapeake Bay; what lives in a river, like smallmouth bass.

g3_sci.title: Snow and Storms
g3_sci.plan: Heavy snow near Lake Erie and Pennsylvania's tornadoes; keep a weather chart and make a safety plan.

g45_sci.title: Franklin and Electricity
g45_sci.plan: Static electricity, lightning, and how a lightning rod works; test simple circuits and discuss Franklin's inventions.

g45_sci.title: Energy from the Ground
g45_sci.plan: How coal and oil form, Pennsylvania's coal mining and the birth of the oil industry, and the trade-offs of using fossil fuels.

g45_sci.title: Watersheds and the Chesapeake
g45_sci.plan: Map the Susquehanna watershed, measure how land use affects water, and explain why Pennsylvania's rivers matter to the Chesapeake Bay.
